questions.question: What are the differences between ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, and Ingress in Kubernetes?
questions.title: Kubernetes Service Types: ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer vs Ingress
questions.direct_answer: ClusterIP: internal-only cluster DNS, no external access (default). NodePort: exposes service on each node's IP + a static port. LoadBalancer: provisions a cloud load balancer with an external IP. Ingress: HTTP/HTTPS routing rules managed by an Ingress controller — the standard way to expose multiple services externally via a single load balancer.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Kubernetes networking and the progression from internal to external service exposure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a LoadBalancer service for every microservice — each provisions a separate cloud load balancer (expensive); use Ingress with ClusterIP services instead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Ingress controllers (nginx-ingress, AWS ALB), TLS termination at Ingress, and how path-based routing works to serve multiple services from one external IP

sections.title: The $500/Month Mistake: One LoadBalancer Per Microservice
sections.content:
A team running ten Spring Boot microservices on AWS creates a LoadBalancer Service for each one. Every `type: LoadBalancer` provisions a separate AWS Network Load Balancer — at roughly $16/month each plus data transfer costs, that is $160/month in infrastructure that serves no purpose. The correct architecture uses a single Ingress controller backed by one load balancer, with all ten services behind ClusterIP.

This mistake reveals a misunderstanding of the **Kubernetes service type hierarchy**. The four types — ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, and Ingress — form a progression from internal-only to external exposure. Each higher level builds on the one below it: a LoadBalancer automatically creates a NodePort, which automatically creates a ClusterIP. Understanding this layering prevents both over-exposure (making internal services externally reachable) and over-spending (provisioning unnecessary cloud resources).

For Java backend architectures, the decision is almost always simple. Internal microservice-to-microservice traffic uses ClusterIP exclusively — these services have no business being reachable from outside the cluster. External traffic enters through a single Ingress controller that routes by host or path to the appropriate internal ClusterIP Service. The only time you need a standalone LoadBalancer Service is for non-HTTP protocols like gRPC or raw TCP that Ingress controllers do not handle natively.

sections.title: From Internal to External: What Each Type Actually Does
sections.content:
Each service type provides a different level of network accessibility, and the cost and complexity increase at each level.

| Type | Reachable From | Mechanism | Cloud Cost | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ClusterIP | Inside cluster only | Virtual IP + DNS | None | Service-to-service calls |
| NodePort | Node IP + high port (30000-32767) | Opens port on every node | None | Dev/testing, bare-metal clusters |
| LoadBalancer | External IP | Cloud-provisioned LB (ALB, NLB) | ~$16+/month each | Single non-HTTP service needing external access |
| Ingress | External via HTTP/HTTPS | Ingress controller + routing rules | One LB shared across all services | Multiple HTTP services, TLS termination, path routing |

**NodePort** deserves special mention because it is rarely the right choice in cloud environments. It exposes your service on every node's IP at a high port — workable for local development with Minikube but operationally painful in production where you would need to manage node IP discovery, health checking, and firewall rules yourself.

**Ingress is not a Service type** — it is a separate Kubernetes resource that defines HTTP routing rules. An Ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, or the AWS ALB Ingress Controller) watches these rules and configures its own load balancer accordingly. One Ingress controller handles routing for every external-facing service in the cluster.

sections.title: The Production Pattern: Ingress Plus ClusterIP for Everything Else
sections.content:
In a production Spring Boot microservices architecture, the networking pattern is consistent. Every service runs as ClusterIP, and a single Ingress controller manages external access.

Internal **east-west traffic** between services uses ClusterIP DNS names. When `order-service` calls `payment-service`, it resolves `payment-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` to a virtual IP. Kube-proxy distributes requests across healthy pods using iptables or IPVS. No external networking is involved — traffic stays inside the cluster network with minimal latency.

External **north-south traffic** from users and API consumers enters through the Ingress controller. A typical Ingress resource routes different URL paths to different backend services.

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.example.com]
      secretName: tls-cert
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: {name: order-svc, port: {number: 80}}
          - path: /payments
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: {name: payment-svc, port: {number: 80}}
```

This single Ingress resource routes `/orders` to the order service and `/payments` to the payment service, all sharing one cloud load balancer. **TLS termination** happens at the Ingress level using a certificate stored in a Kubernetes Secret, so individual services do not need to handle HTTPS themselves. The cost saving compared to one LoadBalancer per service is significant — and the centralized TLS and routing configuration is operationally simpler.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ClusterIP is the default and correct choice for internal traffic** — microservices call each other via DNS names like `payment-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` without any external network exposure
- **One LoadBalancer per service is a costly anti-pattern** — each `type: LoadBalancer` provisions a separate cloud LB; ten services means ten LBs with ten monthly bills when one Ingress controller handles all of them
- **Ingress is not a Service type** — it is a separate Kubernetes resource defining HTTP routing rules processed by an Ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, AWS ALB) that shares one load balancer across all services
- **TLS termination belongs at the Ingress layer** — store certificates as Kubernetes Secrets and configure them in the Ingress spec so individual services do not need to handle HTTPS or certificate management
- **NodePort is a development convenience, not a production solution** — it exposes services on high ports (30000-32767) across all nodes and requires external health checking and firewall management that Ingress handles automatically

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes has four ways to expose a Service, and the choice determines both who can reach it and how traffic enters the cluster. Most teams never use NodePort in production; they use ClusterIP for internal services and a LoadBalancer-backed Ingress for external traffic.

**ClusterIP — internal cluster communication**
- ClusterIP is the default and creates a virtual IP reachable only from within the cluster — services talk to each other using this address; `payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local` resolves to the ClusterIP via CoreDNS
- This is the correct type for every service that should not be reachable from outside the cluster — databases, internal APIs, caches; using anything higher for these is a security exposure

**NodePort — fixed port on every node**
- NodePort opens a port (30000–32767) on every node's IP; traffic to `<any-node-ip>:<nodeport>` reaches the Service — useful for local development without a load balancer (like minikube) but exposes a high port on every node in production
- Production concerns: direct node IP exposure, the port range is inconvenient, and a node IP changes when the node restarts — NodePort is rarely appropriate for production external traffic

**LoadBalancer — cloud load balancer per service**
- `type: LoadBalancer` provisions a cloud load balancer per Service in platforms like AWS EKS, GKE, and AKS — traffic enters the cluster through the cloud load balancer's external IP
- The cost issue: one cloud load balancer per Service at $20–100/month each is expensive for a cluster with 20 Services — this is exactly the problem Ingress solves

**Ingress — one load balancer, many services**
- An Ingress resource defines HTTP(S) routing rules (path-based or host-based) to multiple backend Services behind a single cloud load balancer running the Ingress controller (nginx, AWS ALB, Traefik)
- Ingress handles TLS termination with certificates from cert-manager — the controller presents the correct certificate and routes decrypted traffic to the backend Service; individual Services remain ClusterIP
- The Ingress controller must be installed separately — `kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/...` installs the nginx controller; this is the piece developers most commonly forget when setting up a new cluster

questions.question: How does Kubernetes networking enable pods on different nodes to communicate?
questions.title: Kubernetes Pod Networking: How Pods Communicate Across Nodes
questions.direct_answer: Kubernetes requires every pod to have a routable IP address and be able to communicate with every other pod without NAT, regardless of which node they're on. CNI plugins (Calico, Flannel, Cilium) implement this by creating virtual networks — either overlay (VXLAN tunneling between nodes) or underlay (BGP routing the pod IP range directly). Services provide stable DNS and load balancing on top of this.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of how Kubernetes achieves pod-to-pod communication across the cluster
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking pods communicate via Service endpoints always — pod-to-pod direct communication is possible and used by service meshes, StatefulSet members, and some frameworks
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the CNI plugin concept, contrast overlay (VXLAN) vs underlay (BGP) networking, mention Cilium's eBPF-based networking as the modern high-performance approach, and describe how NetworkPolicies work at the CNI layer

sections.title: The Networking Contract That Makes Everything Else Work: Every Pod Gets a Routable IP
sections.content:
Kubernetes networking is built on a single, non-negotiable rule: **every pod gets a unique, routable IP address**, and any pod can reach any other pod using that IP without NAT. This is fundamentally different from Docker's default networking, where containers share the host's IP and communicate through port mapping. In Kubernetes, pods have their own IPs regardless of which node they run on.

The mechanism that implements this guarantee is the **CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin** — a replaceable component that the cluster operator installs. Flannel, Calico, and Cilium are the three most common choices, and they implement the same contract differently. Some wrap pod traffic in tunnels that traverse the existing network (overlay). Others configure the physical network to route pod IP ranges directly (underlay). The application code does not know or care which approach is used — it just connects to pod IPs.

For Java backend developers, the practical impact shows up in debugging: when a service cannot reach another service, understanding whether the problem is DNS resolution (Service layer), pod-to-pod routing (CNI layer), or pod health (readiness probe) determines where to look first. Most application-level connectivity issues are DNS or label mismatches, not CNI problems — but when the CNI is the problem, the symptoms look identical to application bugs: timeouts, connection refused, intermittent failures.

sections.title: Overlay Mode: How VXLAN Wraps Pod Traffic for Any Network
sections.content:
The simplest CNI approach is **overlay networking**, where pod-to-pod traffic between nodes is encapsulated inside regular UDP packets. Flannel's VXLAN mode is the most common implementation of this pattern.

Each node gets a pod CIDR from the cluster's overall pod network — for example, node 1 gets `10.244.1.0/24` and node 2 gets `10.244.2.0/24`. Pods on node 1 get IPs from the first range, pods on node 2 from the second. When pod `10.244.1.5` on node 1 sends a packet to pod `10.244.2.8` on node 2, the traffic follows this path: the packet leaves the pod's virtual ethernet interface, hits the `cni0` bridge on node 1, reaches the **`flannel.1` VXLAN device**, which wraps the entire packet inside a UDP frame addressed to node 2's real IP. The underlying network routes this UDP packet normally. On node 2, the `flannel.1` device unwraps it and delivers the original packet to the destination pod.

The **advantage** is portability — VXLAN works on any network that can route UDP between nodes. No special switch configuration, no BGP, no cloud-specific features required. The **cost** is overhead: every packet gets an additional 50-byte VXLAN header, and the encapsulation and decapsulation adds CPU load. For most Spring Boot microservices, this overhead is negligible — measured in single-digit microseconds per packet — but for high-throughput data pipelines moving gigabytes per second, it becomes significant.

sections.title: Native Routing and eBPF: When Performance Demands Eliminating the Tunnel
sections.content:
**Calico with BGP** and **Cilium with eBPF** both avoid encapsulation overhead by making the physical network aware of pod IP ranges. Instead of tunneling, they configure routing tables so pod traffic flows directly through the network fabric.

Calico runs a BGP daemon on each node that advertises its pod CIDR to the network's routers. When pod `10.244.1.5` sends traffic to `10.244.2.8`, node 1's routing table says: `10.244.2.0/24 via node-2-IP`. The packet travels through the network's standard routing — no encapsulation, no overhead. The prerequisite is a network that supports BGP or a cloud provider offering VPC-native pod networking (GKE, EKS with VPC CNI).

**Cilium** takes a different approach using **eBPF** (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) — programs that run directly in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Instead of generating iptables rules (which Calico and kube-proxy use and which become slow at thousands of entries), Cilium attaches eBPF programs to network hooks. These programs make routing decisions at kernel speed without the overhead of matching against a long chain of iptables rules. Cilium also provides **Hubble** for network observability — real-time flow logs showing which pods are communicating, on which ports, with what latency.

**NetworkPolicies** are enforced at the CNI level regardless of which plugin you use. A NetworkPolicy restricts which pods can communicate with which — by default, most clusters allow all pod-to-pod traffic. Defining a deny-all default policy with explicit allow rules implements microsegmentation, limiting lateral movement if a pod is compromised. The CNI plugin translates NetworkPolicy resources into actual packet filtering rules at the kernel level.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Every pod gets a unique routable IP without NAT** — the fundamental Kubernetes networking contract; CNI plugins implement this guarantee, and application code never manages port mapping or host IP addresses
- **Overlay (VXLAN) works on any network but adds encapsulation overhead** — Flannel wraps pod packets in UDP frames; the 50-byte header and CPU cost are negligible for typical REST services but matter for data-intensive pipelines
- **Calico BGP routes pod CIDRs through the network fabric directly** — eliminates tunnel overhead by advertising pod IP ranges to routers, but requires BGP-capable switches or cloud VPC-native networking support
- **Cilium uses eBPF programs instead of iptables chains** — kernel-level packet processing scales better than iptables at thousands of rules; also provides Hubble for real-time network observability and flow logging
- **NetworkPolicies default to allow-all in most clusters** — without explicit deny-all policies, any pod can reach any other pod; microsegmentation requires defining ingress and egress rules enforced by the CNI plugin

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes networking is built on a flat network model: every Pod gets its own IP address and every Pod can reach every other Pod by IP across any node, without NAT. The CNI plugin is the software that implements this model on real hardware.

**The flat network model**
- Every Pod in the cluster has a unique IP address from the Pod CIDR; Pods on different nodes communicate directly using these IPs without port mapping or NAT — this simplicity is what makes DNS-based service discovery predictable and service mesh routing reliable
- The `kube-proxy` on each node maintains iptables or IPVS rules that translate a ClusterIP Service address to one of the backend Pod IPs — this is how `payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local` resolves to a stable virtual IP that then load-balances to actual Pod IPs

**CNI plugins — the implementation layer**
- The Container Network Interface (CNI) spec defines how Kubernetes networking is plugged in — Calico, Flannel, Cilium, and Weave are all CNI implementations; your cluster runs one
- Calico uses BGP to advertise Pod routes between nodes — each node's Pod subnet is a BGP route; Pods route directly to each other across nodes at near-native speed without encapsulation overhead
- Cilium uses eBPF instead of iptables for packet routing — eBPF programs run in the kernel and bypass the iptables layer entirely, providing better performance and more flexible policy enforcement; newer managed Kubernetes offerings are migrating to Cilium

**Network Policies — the access control layer**
- Without Network Policies, every Pod can reach every other Pod on any port cluster-wide — a security risk in multi-team clusters
- Network Policies are additive: a Policy that allows ingress from the `payments` namespace is combined with any other Policies on that Pod; there is no default-deny until you explicitly create a default-deny Policy
- Start with a default-deny-all ingress policy per namespace, then add explicit allow rules for the traffic you want — this is the only approach that provides meaningful isolation; relying on no-policy means any future mistake opens traffic across all namespaces
